312.t: Dixieland revival and New York clubs as teenagers
312.s: Andre explains how they saw the music as live, not dated, going to Condon and Jimmy Ryan's and listening to records.
312.q: No. I really didn’t think of it as dated, and I lived in New York there, on Long Island, and the clubs in New York City which were experiencing the Dixieland revival period, if you will, the Condon band and Max Kaminsky and there was Nick’s in Central Plaza and Jimmy Ryan’s — there was a whole lot…

312.t: Condon band swing, two-beat feel and his banjo style
312.s: Andre did not distinguish black and white jazz, disliked Armstrong then, and prized Condon's swinging guitar and two-beat drive.
312.q: No. There really wasn’t. In fact, because my introduction to it, if you will, was through the bands who were playing Dixieland and traditional jazz in the late 40s and 50s, I really didn’t pay much attention to the earlier stuff. In fact some of the records, and some of my

91.t: New Orleans music's influence in New York
91.s: New Orleans players were respected in New York but Carter doubts they changed New York music.
91.ch: Harlem scene and race in music
91.q: No doubt they did. I couldn't site any particular examples, you know, but ...

91.t: Records, New Orleans and Chicago music reaching New York
91.s: Carter and Patrick discuss which records New York musicians heard, from King Oliver to Piron, and New York as a melting pot.
91.q: Richmond, Indiana, I guess. We didn't hear too much of Earl Hines until later, after he had gone to join Louis Armstrong, that is.

53.t: How New Orleans jazz spread north and Oliver's influence
53.s: Billy says the beat reached other places only when New Orleans men spread out, Chicago first. Local musicians were puzzled, crowds of players listened at the Royal Garden, and the traveling shows gave many their start.

23.t: Original Dixieland Jazz Band's impact on northern musicians
23.s: Rose says jazz is indigenous to New Orleans; the Original Dixieland Jazz Band's 1916 success led northern readers to imitate it, and Kansas City bands orchestrated the blues.
23.q: uh from the time when the original Dixieland jazz band yeah um made their appearance in 1916 in Risenwebers yeah uh their impact on the on the popular musicians of the east was enormous uh and uh and their presence uh uh exercised uh incalculable effect now uh it's perfectly natural that that…

743.t: How Dixieland changed: classic jazz, Chicago style and the revivalists
743.s: Gordon dislikes the term Dixieland, tracing the music from 1920s black New Orleans artists through white Chicago players, the move to New York, and the 1960s revivalists like Marty Grosz.
743.q: Well it’s changed quite a bit. In the old days, I guess in New Orleans in the 1920s and even before that, they called it Dixieland jazz and they had mostly blacks playing that

842.t: Listening habits: New York Dixieland versus traditional jazz
842.s: They listened to the New York scene, not Turk Murphy or Kid Ory, which Mead now explores.
842.q: But just to finish up one thing, so we didn’t think of ourselves in the Catatonic Five as playing traditional jazz. And we frankly didn’t listen to a lot of traditional jazz. I mean we were much more listening to the stuff that was going on in New York, so Turk Murphy and Kid Ory and stuff like…

448.t: The Wildcats as revivalists versus the Condon style
448.s: They emulated Oliver, Morton and Armstrong from records, unlike the Chicago players who heard them live.
448.q: Well in a sense we did because we were immersed in the music of King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton, Armstrong Hot Five, and we wanted to play in that style. We didn’t want to imitate their records. We wanted to play in their style but be creative at the same time. And yeah, in a sense it was quite…

147.t: Hearing Chick Webb, Kaiser Marshall and Zutty after reaching New York
147.s: Crawford says he heard Chick Webb nightly in New York and describes Zutty's New Orleans style.
147.ch: Learning the drums and early influences
147.q: He played mostly Dixieland with hitting on (Inaudible) and his bass drum, you know, cowbells and things like that. That, to me, was the New Orleans style.
